lead: A Yagi-Uda antenna gets a directional beam from one driven dipole and a row of passive rods that are not connected to the feed. It is cheap and compact, gives about 7–15 dBi, but only over a narrow band. A log-periodic dipole array takes the opposite trade: many dipoles of different lengths, each handling a small slice of frequency, so one antenna covers a wide band. Yagis sit on rooftops for TV and inside RFID readers; log-periodic arrays serve EMC measurement, HF radio and TV reception.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for pattern multiplication, Chapter 3.2 for end-fire arrays, and the half-wave and folded dipole from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Shintaro Uda built this array in 1920s Japan and Hidetsugu Yagi published it, so both names stick; the short form Yagi is common. One element is driven: a half-wave dipole, often a folded dipole, because its input impedance near 300 Ω suits a twin-line feeder (Unit 2). Every other rod is parasitic: mounted on the boom, insulated from it, and not wired to the feed.

items: Driven element: 0.47λ to 0.48λ long, where λ is the free-space wavelength at the design frequency.
Reflector: placed behind the driven element, 0.50λ to 0.55λ long, spaced 0.15λ to 0.25λ away.
Directors: placed in front, 0.40λ to 0.45λ long, each slightly shorter than the previous one, spaced about 0.2λ to 0.4λ apart.
Gain: about 7 dBi with one reflector and one director, 9–11 dBi for five elements, up to about 15 dBi for very long arrays.
Bandwidth: only 2–5% of the design frequency.

blocks.text: Feeding is simple: one cable, no power dividers, no phase shifters. That is why a Yagi costs a few hundred rupees and hangs on every Indian rooftop for Doordarshan and cable TV reception.

sections.h3: Why the beam points at the directors

blocks.text: Parasitic does not mean inactive. The field of the driven element induces a current in every rod, and each rod re-radiates. The total pattern is the element pattern multiplied by an array factor set by those induced currents (Chapter 3.1). Element length and spacing fix the phase of each current.

The reflector is longer than resonance, so its current lags. Placed about 0.2λ behind, its re-radiated field cancels the driven element's field to the rear and adds to it in front. Directors are shorter than resonance, so their currents lead, and the spacing is chosen so that their fields add toward the front. The result is an end-fire array (Chapter 3.2), firing along the boom away from the reflector.

Because the phases come from geometry, not from a feed network, a Yagi cannot be retuned after it is built. Adding directors raises gain with diminishing returns, and each added director narrows the band further.

A log-periodic antenna repeats its shape at scaled sizes, so its properties stay roughly constant over frequency. In the dipole version, the LPDA, parallel dipoles get steadily shorter from back to front and the spacings shrink with them.

blocks.where: τ is the scaling factor, dimensionless, typically 0.7 to 0.95; L(n) is the length of the n-th dipole counting from the longest at the rear.
σ is the spacing factor, dimensionless, typically 0.06 to 0.2; d(n) is the gap between dipole n and dipole n+1; L(n) is the length of dipole n.

blocks.text: All dipoles are fed from a two-wire line along the boom, with the connections crossed between neighbours so adjacent dipoles are driven in antiphase. Only the dipoles near resonance, with L close to λ/2, carry large current: this is the active region. At the lowest frequency the longest rear dipole is active; as frequency rises the active region moves toward the short front end. The longest dipole works at the lowest frequency, never the reverse.
N = 1 + ln(B) / ln(1/τ), where B = fmax / fmin
blocks.where: N is the number of elements, rounded up to a whole number; B is the bandwidth ratio, dimensionless; fmax and fmin are the band edges in Hz; τ is the scaling factor.

blocks.text: A printed variant, the log-periodic tooth antenna, uses triangular teeth on a microstrip line and is common in TV and EMC work.

items: Fix the band and compute B = fmax / fmin.
Pick τ (0.8 to 0.9 is a common compromise between size and gain).
Compute N = 1 + ln(B)/ln(1/τ) and round up.
Set the longest dipole to about half a wavelength at fmin: L(1) = 150 / fmin, with fmin in MHz and L(1) in metres.
Find the shortest dipole from L(N) = L(1) τ^(N−1).
Choose σ (near 0.15 for moderate gain) and lay out the boom.

figure.caption: Dipole lengths of a 12-element log-periodic array with τ = 0.9 and the longest dipole at 750 mm. The shortest element is about 235 mm, and it takes over when the active region reaches the front of the boom.

spec.aria: Log-periodic dipole lengths for τ = 0.9 from 750 mm; the shortest of 12 elements is about 235 mm.

examples.question: A log-periodic dipole array must cover 200 MHz to 600 MHz. Use τ = 0.9 and a longest dipole of 750 mm. Find the bandwidth ratio, the number of elements and the length of the shortest dipole.
steps: Bandwidth ratio: B = fmax / fmin = 600 MHz / 200 MHz = 3, dimensionless.
Shortest dipole: L(12) = 750 mm × 0.9¹¹. Now 0.9¹¹ = 0.3138, so L(12) = 235.4 mm.
Check the longest dipole: 750 mm is half a wavelength at 200 MHz, since λ = 300/200 = 1.5 m = 1500 mm and 1500/2 = 750 mm. The design is consistent.
examples.answer: B = 3, N = 12 elements, and the shortest dipole is about 235 mm.
examples.check:
import math
fmin = 200e6
fmax = 600e6
tau = 0.9
L1 = 750
B = fmax / fmin
N_raw = 1 + math.log(B) / math.log(1 / tau)
N = math.ceil(N_raw)
Lmin = L1 * tau ** (N - 1)
print(round(B, 2))
print(round(N_raw, 2))
print(N)
print(round(Lmin, 2))

traps: Do not call the Yagi wideband. Its bandwidth is a few percent, and adding directors narrows it further.
In an LPDA the longest dipole works at the lowest frequency. The active region moves to the short front elements as frequency rises.
The reflector is not a mirror or a dish. It is a rod slightly longer than resonance that re-radiates with the right phase.
Do not swap τ and σ: τ compares adjacent dipole lengths, σ compares spacing with length.
Gain in dBd is relative to a half-wave dipole, so dBi = dBd + 2.15 dB. Mixing the two inflates the answer by over 2 dB.

quiz.q: In a Yagi-Uda array, is the reflector longer or shorter than the driven element, and where is it placed?
quiz.a: Longer, by about 5% (0.50λ to 0.55λ), placed behind the driven element at 0.15λ to 0.25λ.

quiz.q: Define the scaling factor τ and the spacing factor σ of an LPDA.
quiz.a: τ = L(n+1)/L(n), the ratio of adjacent dipole lengths, typically 0.7 to 0.95. σ = d(n)/(2L(n)), the spacing to twice the length, typically 0.06 to 0.2.

quiz.q: Why is the Yagi's bandwidth only a few percent even when more directors are added?
quiz.a: The beam depends on the induced currents having the right phase, and that phase holds only near the design frequency. More directors sharpen the array factor and narrow the band further, so gain and bandwidth trade against each other.

quiz.q: What is meant by the active region of an LPDA, and why does it move?
quiz.a: The few dipoles whose length is near λ/2 carry large current and radiate most of the power. As frequency rises, the half-wave length falls, so the resonant group shifts toward the shorter elements at the front of the boom.

quiz.q: An LPDA must cover 100 MHz to 1000 MHz with τ = 0.85. Find B and the number of elements.
An LPDA has a longest dipole of 600 mm, τ = 0.9 and 10 elements. Find the shortest dipole.
A Yagi cut for 400 MHz is used at 450 MHz. What happens to gain, pattern and input impedance?
quiz.a: Every element is now electrically longer than designed, so the induced-current phases are wrong. Gain falls, the beam tilts and sidelobes grow, and the driven element no longer looks like a matched dipole, so VSWR rises.

quiz.q: Why are adjacent LPDA dipoles fed in antiphase?
quiz.a: The dipoles are about λ/4 apart in the active region. The antiphase feed adds a 180° step between neighbours, which combines with the propagation phase to make the active-region fields add toward the short front end, giving an end-fire beam.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial Yagis are now optimised by numerical electromagnetics rather than the old cut-and-try lengths, and the same solvers design LPDA booms for EMC chambers that must hold gain flat from 200 MHz to 3 GHz. Printed log-periodic teeth appear in broadband TV and monitoring antennas, and quasi-log-periodic designs are used in tightly packed phased arrays. Search for LPDA design tables (τ, σ, boom length), Yagi director optimisation, and log-periodic tooth antennas if you want the design side.
